title: Iterators and yield (deferred sequences)
hook: yield return does not run your method body right away. It builds a state machine that executes one item at a time when the caller loops — that is why a CSV import can look instant and then fail on the first foreach.

blocks.text: An iterator method uses yield return to produce items lazily — one at a time, on demand. The compiler transforms your method into a state machine class that remembers where it paused. The method returns immediately with an IEnumerable<T> object; the actual work happens when the consumer calls MoveNext. yield break ends the sequence early. You cannot mix yield return with a normal return of a collection in the same method.

entries.plainDefinition: A method that uses yield return or yield break to produce a sequence lazily, one item per MoveNext call.
entries.example: IEnumerable<string> ReadLines(string path) { yield return line; }

entries.plainDefinition: Pauses the method and hands one item to the caller. The method resumes after that item is consumed.
entries.example: yield return row; pauses until the next foreach iteration.

entries.plainDefinition: Work that is postponed until someone actually asks for the next item — not when the method is called.
entries.example: ReadCsvRows(path) returns immediately; the file opens on the first MoveNext.

entries.plainDefinition: A nested class the compiler creates to store local variables and the resume point between yield returns.
entries.example: Your simple while loop becomes a class with a switch on the current state.

blocks.text: Deferred execution lets you process a 400,000-line CSV without loading it all into memory first. LINQ is built entirely on this model — Where, Select, and Take all stack iterators. The danger: calling Count() then foreach enumerates twice. If the source is a network stream or a non-rewindable resource, the second pass is empty or throws. Exceptions from the iterator body surface at MoveNext, not when you called the method.

blocks.title: Two foreach calls, two executions
blocks.body: Each foreach creates a new enumerator and re-runs the iterator from the start. To snapshot, call ToList() once, then walk the list as many times as you need.

sections.heading: How yield works step by step

items.title: Call the iterator method
items.body: var rows = ReadCsvRows(path); returns immediately. No file I/O has happened yet.

items.title: First MoveNext (first foreach)
items.body: The state machine runs until the first yield return, producing one item. The file opens here.

items.title: Subsequent MoveNext calls
items.body: Each call resumes after the previous yield return until yield break or the method ends.

items.title: Dispose cleans up
items.body: When the enumerator is disposed (foreach does this), any using blocks inside the iterator run their cleanup.

snippet.label: CSV rows yielded, not buffered
snippet.explanation: The using block keeps the file open for the lifetime of the enumerator. Dispose (called by foreach) closes the file when iteration ends.

snippet.label: Deferred call versus enumeration
snippet.explanation: Each foreach creates a new enumerator and re-executes the iterator from scratch. To snapshot, materialize once: var snapshot = rows.ToList();

snippet.label: Materialize to avoid double enumeration
snippet.explanation: ToList() forces full enumeration and stores every item in memory. Use this when you know you will walk the data more than once.

snippet.label: Exception surfaces at MoveNext, not at call
snippet.explanation: Iterator exceptions appear at the consumer's MoveNext call site, not where you invoked the iterator method. Stack traces confuse interviewers and production on-call engineers alike.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Disposing the StreamReader before the caller enumerates — the iterator needs the stream alive. Using yield to wrap a List you already built — you added a state machine for no benefit. Assuming iterator exceptions happen at the call site — they surface at MoveNext when the consumer pulls the next item.

blocks.text: The compiler transforms a yield method into a nested class implementing IEnumerator<T> with a state field (0 = start, -1 = done, N = resume point), local variable copies, and a switch on state in MoveNext. Each yield return becomes a state transition; yield break sets state to -1. The iterator object is a heap allocation even before the first MoveNext. How to prove it in production: BenchmarkDotNet comparing yield-based CSV read versus ReadLines + ToList; dotnet-counters gen-0-gc-count when callers enumerate the same IEnumerable twice instead of materializing once.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: One item at a time, low peak memory
Caller will enumerate twice or needs Count
Infinite or very large streams where streaming wins
Async pull, one item at a time
Sync-only callers — use yield or List
Composed iterators, no work until MoveNext
Side effects or I/O hidden in Select/Where
List already in memory — return the List directly

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying "yield is free — it is just lazy" — it allocates a state machine class on the heap. Saying "I'll call Count() then foreach" on a database-backed iterator — that is two full passes. Strong answer: yield for streaming large inputs once; ToList when multiple passes needed; IAsyncEnumerable for async pull (module 13).

interviewTakeaways: yield return compiles to a state machine class; the method body runs lazily on MoveNext.
Each foreach creates a new enumerator and re-executes from the start — ToList for snapshots.
Iterator exceptions surface at MoveNext in the caller's stack, not at the iterator method call.

60s: yield is deferred execution via a compiler-generated state machine. Stream large CSV once with yield. Materialize with ToList if you enumerate twice. Async streams are IAsyncEnumerable — module 13.
Follow-up: can you mix yield return and return in the same method? (no — compiler error)
commonPitfalls: Saying yield is free — it allocates a heap state machine even before the first MoveNext.
Strong answer: yield for single-pass streaming; ToList when multiple enumerations needed; never Count() then foreach on I/O-backed sequences.
Disposing StreamReader before the caller enumerates — iterator needs the stream alive.
Using yield to wrap a List already in memory — adds state machine overhead for zero benefit.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS generators are the same deferred idea. for...of pulls. Re-iterating a generator that already finished is empty unless you call the factory again.
async function* maps to IAsyncEnumerable in C# (module 13), not to Task<IEnumerable<T>>.
function* and yield in JS are the closest analog to C# iterator methods.
